title: Given k sorted lists, merge them into one sorted list efficiently using a priority queue (heap).
shortTitle: Merge K Sorted Lists Using a Min-Heap
topicTitle: Write a function that counts the number of set bits

s1_definition.profdef: Merging k sorted lists produces a single sorted output by repeatedly taking the smallest unconsumed element across all lists. A min-heap holding one candidate from each list makes "find the current smallest" a logarithmic operation: you poll the smallest, append it to the output, and push the next element from the list that element came from. With N total elements and k lists, this runs in N log k time and k extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has k branch ledgers, each already sorted by transaction time, and wants one combined ledger in time order. A clerk looks only at the earliest unprocessed entry from each branch, picks the single earliest among them, writes it into the combined ledger, then looks at the next entry from just that branch. She keeps a tiny sorted tray with one entry per branch so finding the earliest is instant. She never re-reads entries she has already filed, so the work is proportional to the total entries, not to re-scanning every branch each time.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep one candidate per list in a min-heap; poll the smallest, output it, and push that list's next element, for N log k total.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Merging k sorted lists produces a single sorted output by repeatedly taking the smallest unconsumed element across all lists. A min-heap holding one candidate from each list makes "find the current smallest" a logarithmic operation: you poll the smallest, append it to the output, and push the next element from the list that element came from. With N total elements and k lists, this runs in N log k time and k extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has k branch ledgers, each already sorted by transaction time, and wants one combined ledger in time order. A clerk looks only at the earliest unprocessed entry from each branch, picks the single earliest among them, writes it into the combined ledger, then looks at the next entry from just that branch. She keeps a tiny sorted tray with one entry per branch so finding the earliest is instant. She never re-reads entries she has already filed, so the work is proportional to the total entries, not to re-scanning every branch each time.

**One line to remember:** Keep one candidate per list in a min-heap; poll the smallest, output it, and push that list's next element, for N log k total.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach concatenates all lists and sorts, which is N log N. A smarter observation is that each list is already sorted, so you only ever need to compare the current fronts of the k lists. That reduces the comparison work from log N to log k per element.

The heap holds at most k elements, one from each list, ordered by value. You seed it with the first element of each non-empty list. Then you loop: `poll` the smallest, append it to the result, and if the list it came from has a next element, `offer` that next element. Because the heap only ever holds one representative per list, its size stays at most k, so each poll and offer is log k. You repeat until the heap is empty, having emitted all N elements in sorted order.

To know which list an element came from, you wrap each value with its source, for example an index plus position, or in a linked-list version you push the node itself and follow its next pointer. In Java you build the heap with a comparator over the stored value, for example `new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparing(entry -> entry.value))`. For money the value is a BigDecimal compared with compareTo.

A senior-level nuance is the alternative divide-and-conquer merge, which pairs up lists and merges them two at a time in log k rounds, also achieving N log k but without an explicit heap. The heap version is simpler to reason about and streams naturally, which is why it is the common interview answer, and it is exactly how an external multi-way merge sort combines sorted runs from disk, a technique banks use to merge large sorted transaction files.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India receives end-of-day transaction files from several branches, each already sorted by amount, and must produce one globally sorted file for settlement. Concatenating and re-sorting everything wastes the fact that each file is already ordered. This is exactly the k-way merge with a heap, because we only ever compare the current fronts.

Problem 2 — The combined feed can be very large, so we want memory bounded to the number of branches, not the total number of transactions. A heap holding one entry per branch keeps memory at k regardless of total size.

In our mini-project we build a `LedgerMerger` that merges several sorted lists of BigDecimal amounts into one sorted list using a PriorityQueue with source tracking. The demo merges three branch lists and logs the merged output.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three sorted branch lists, the first hundred, five hundred, nine hundred; the second two hundred, four hundred; the third fifty, six hundred, one thousand.

Step 1: Seed the heap with the first element of each list: hundred from list zero, two hundred from list one, fifty from list two. The heap orders them, so the smallest ready is fifty.

Step 2: Poll fifty, append it to the result, and push the next element from list two, which is six hundred. The heap now holds hundred, two hundred, six hundred.

Step 3: Poll hundred, append it, push the next from list zero, which is five hundred. The heap holds two hundred, five hundred, six hundred.

Step 4: Poll two hundred, append, push four hundred from list one. The heap holds four hundred, five hundred, six hundred. Poll four hundred, append, list one is now exhausted so nothing is pushed.

Step 5: Continue polling five hundred, then six hundred and pushing one thousand from list two, then nine hundred from list zero, then one thousand. Each poll emits the next smallest across all lists.

Step 6: The heap empties after emitting all eight elements in sorted order: fifty, hundred, two hundred, four hundred, five hundred, six hundred, nine hundred, one thousand. The heap never held more than three entries, confirming memory bounded to k.

```
[2026-10-26 23:26:01] INFO    Merged sorted ledger: [50, 100, 200, 400, 500, 600, 900, 1000]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Merging k sorted lists means producing one sorted output by repeatedly taking the smallest element that has not yet been consumed across all the lists. The naive way concatenates everything and sorts, which is N log N, but that throws away the fact that each list is already ordered. The key insight is that I only ever need to compare the current fronts of the k lists, and a min-heap makes finding the smallest front a log k operation.

The mechanics are a clean loop. I seed the heap with the first element of each non-empty list, so it holds one candidate per list. Then I poll the smallest, append it to the output, and push the next element from whichever list that one came from. Because the heap only ever holds one representative per list, its size stays at most k, so every poll and push is log k, and over all N elements the total is N log k with only k extra space. To know which list to advance, I wrap each value in a small entry that records its source list and position.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to merge end-of-day transaction files from several branches, each already sorted, into one globally sorted file for settlement. The heap holds one entry per branch, so memory stays bounded to the number of branches no matter how many total transactions flow through, which matters because the combined feed is large.

The senior-level point I make is that there is an equivalent divide-and-conquer approach that merges lists pairwise in log k rounds, also N log k, but the heap version is simpler to reason about and streams naturally. I also note that this is exactly how external merge sort combines sorted runs from disk, which is the real technique banks use to merge enormous sorted transaction files that do not fit in memory, so the interview problem maps directly onto production batch processing.
